title: The historical debate over nondelegation
summary: The editors describe competing originalist claims and early statutes whose broad discretion complicates a categorical historical account.
notes:
The assigned discussion distinguishes evidence that some limit on delegation existed from evidence identifying that limit precisely. Early Supreme Court treatment was sparse. Scholars disagree about founding-era statements, their acceptance, and their relevance to contemporary administrative power. The source attributes competing positions to Mortenson and Bagley, Bamzai, Wurman, Hamburger, Parrillo, and others.

Early examples include discretionary disability benefits, licensing of trade with Native nations, postal administration, embargoes, seamen’s hospitals, and mass adjustment of property-tax assessments. Advocates of categorical limits invoke exceptions for benefits, foreign affairs, or fact-finding; critics question the historical support and boundaries of those exceptions. A looser important-subjects-versus-details test may be harder to falsify historically but may overlap substantially with the intelligible-principle inquiry. These arguments are reported as contested scholarship, not resolved historical facts establishing one constitutional rule.
